stem: During an emergency red-cell transfusion before the recipient's ABO type is known, why may group O red blood cells be selected when considering ABO compatibility?

options.A: Group O red cells are used for emergent initial support when the recipient's ABO group is unknown; Rh and other compatibility factors are considered separately.
options.B: Group O is the universal red-cell recipient group, so a recipient with group O blood can receive red cells from any ABO donor group.
options.C: Group O red cells follow the same compatibility direction as AB plasma, so red-cell and plasma ABO selection can be treated as interchangeable.
options.D: Group O red cells are selected because emergency transfusion removes the need for ABO typing and type-specific red cells after pretransfusion testing is completed.

rationale: Current AABB patient information states that in an emergency anyone can receive type O red blood cells, while individuals of all ABO types can receive type AB plasma, demonstrating that compatibility depends on the blood component. AABB's group O red-cell bulletin further states that group O RBCs are appropriate for emergent/initial transfusion support in patients of unknown blood group and that patients should be switched to type-specific RBCs once pretransfusion testing is complete and compatible blood is available. Therefore A is correct. B reverses donor and recipient concepts, C incorrectly makes plasma and red-cell compatibility interchangeable, and D incorrectly implies that emergency use eliminates subsequent typing/type-specific selection.
educational_objective: Recognize group O red cells as the ABO-compatible emergency red-cell choice when recipient ABO type is not yet known while distinguishing red-cell compatibility from plasma compatibility and separate Rh considerations.
